title: A Confederacy of Dunces
author: John Kennedy Toole
description: Toole's New Orleans is a hot, cluttered comic stage: a medievalist crank in a hunting cap wages war on the modern world from his mother's shotgun house Uptown out to the department-store clock on Canal Street, the neon of Bourbon Street, the French Quarter where he peddles hot dogs, and a failing pants factory down by the river. The map runs from Uptown across the Central Business District and French Quarter to Bywater.

route.displayName: The D.H. Holmes clock, Canal Street
route.summary: The book begins with the hero loitering under a landmark department-store clock, waiting for his mother and sneering at the crowd of shoppers around him. The store is long gone, redeveloped into a hotel, but a bronze figure in a hunting cap now stands under a replica clock to mark where the comedy starts.
route.note: The novel opens by name at the clock outside the D.H. Holmes department store on Canal Street; the store closed in 1989 and the building is now a hotel, with a statue of the hero marking the spot at 819 Canal.

route.summary: The hero lives with his widowed mother in a cramped house on a quiet Uptown street, holed up in a back room writing screeds against the modern age. The author names the street but no address; the humble shotgun houses in the 600 block have long been read as the model for the home.
route.note: Toole names Constantinople Street in Uptown but never gives a number; local research points to the modest shotgun houses in the 600 block of the Touro neighbourhood, so this marks that block.

route.displayName: The Night of Joy, Bourbon Street
route.summary: A seedy Bourbon Street nightclub is the engine of half the plot, with its put-upon barmaid, its scheming owner, and a stripper whose act involves a cockatoo. The bar itself is fiction, but the author sets it firmly on the real Bourbon Street, amid the drink and neon the hero loudly deplores.
route.note: The Night of Joy bar is invented, but the novel plants it explicitly on Bourbon Street in the French Quarter, so this marks a representative point on the strip of neon and clubs.

route.displayName: Levy Pants, down by the river
route.summary: The hero takes a clerical job at a shabby, failing trouser factory downriver, where he promptly launches a doomed workers' crusade and files the correspondence in the bin. The author sites the plant by the river near the Industrial Canal, in the working district now called Bywater.
route.note: Levy Pants is fictional; the novel places it downriver by the Industrial Canal near Poland Avenue, in what is now Bywater, so this marks that riverside stretch. No surviving building matches the described factory.

route.summary: Cast out to earn a living, the hero pushes a hot-dog cart through the French Quarter, eating most of the stock himself and costumed as a pirate to hawk them. The cart wanders the old streets around Jackson Square, the tourist heart of the Quarter, which anchors this stop.
route.note: The novel sets the hero's vending in the French Quarter without fixing one corner, since the cart roams, so this marks the heart of the Quarter at Jackson Square.
